items.prompt: Black to move. The knight on e4 is not attacked yet. Find a developing move that attacks it. Two of the natural moves do; either is accepted.

claims.statement: After ...Nf6 one black piece attacks the knight on e4.
After ...Bf5 one black piece attacks the knight on e4.

hints: Which black pieces could attack the square e4?
A knight and a bishop can each reach a square that attacks e4.
Either the knight goes to f6, or the c8 bishop goes to f5.
items.explain: The knight on f6 attacks e4 by its L-shaped move, and the bishop on f5 attacks it along the diagonal. Both develop a piece with a threat. Which one Black chooses decides which gambit White can play next.

items.prompt: White to move. Tap every square the knight on g5 can move to.

claims.statement: The knight on g5 can go to exactly these squares.

hints: A knight moves two squares one way and one square the other way.
Some of its squares hold black pieces or pawns, and it may capture them.
Five squares: e4, e6, f7, h3 and h7.
items.explain: The knight can capture on f7 or go to h7 or e6, or step back to e4 or to the edge on h3. Most of these squares are attacked by Black; only the retreat to h3 keeps the piece out of immediate danger. That is the choice White faces on move seven.

items.prompt: White to move. Find the move the engine prefers at depth 16. It keeps all the material.

claims.statement: The retreat to h3 is within 40 cp of the engine's top move (depth 16).
The knight sacrifice on e6 is at least 150 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).
The knight sacrifice on f7 is at least 150 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: The knight is attacked by a pawn, and a pawn is worth less than a knight.
One retreat keeps every piece.
The knight goes to h3.
items.explain: The pawn on h6 attacks the knight. Retreating to h3 keeps both knights and loses nothing, but the knight stands near the edge. The two sacrifices, on e6 and on f7, give up a whole knight. Engine, depth 16: the retreat leads, and each sacrifice is at least a pawn and a half behind it.

feedback_by_move.g5e6: This gives up the knight. The next boards show what White hopes to get for it.
feedback_by_move.g5f7: This is the Alien idea, a knight for a pawn. The bishop on g6 changes the position; see the series on that gambit.

items.explain: A knight on e6 reaches c5, c7, d4, d8, f4, f8, g5 and g7. The queen stands on d8 and the bishop on f8, so one jump hits both. The pawn on g7 is attacked too, but a pawn is not what the question asks for.

claims.statement: Taking the knight with the f-pawn is the engine's top move (depth 16).
7...Qd6 is at least 200 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).
7...Qc8 is at least 250 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).
7...Qd7 is at least 250 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).
After 7...Qd6 the knight on e6 attacks the bishop on f8.
After 7...Qd6 only the king defends the bishop on f8, so it can retake.

hints: Which black piece is allowed to capture the knight?
The pawn on f7 attacks e6.
The f-pawn takes on e6.
items.explain: Taking the knight removes the attacker, so neither the queen nor the bishop has to move. If the queen moves instead, the knight takes on f8 and the king retakes: material is level, Black has not won the piece, and the king can no longer castle. Engine, depth 16: taking is best by a wide margin; each queen move is at least two pawns worse.

feedback_by_move.d8d6: The queen escapes, but the knight takes on f8 and the king retakes: material is level, Black can no longer castle, and the engine has White better by about 1.6 (depth 20).
feedback_by_move.d8c8: Same problem: the knight takes on f8 and the king retakes, so Black has not won the piece and cannot castle.
feedback_by_move.d8d7: The queen steps off the knight's reach, but the knight takes on f8 and the king retakes: the piece is not won and the king cannot castle.

items.prompt: Black to move. One black piece is attacked and no black piece defends it. Tap it.

claims.statement: The bishop on g6 is Black's only loose piece.

hints: Look at what the white knight on e5 attacks.
One of the squares it attacks holds a black bishop.
The bishop on g6.
items.explain: The knight on e5 attacks g6. The bishop there was guarded by the f7 pawn before the capture on e6 and by the h7 pawn before ...h6, and now by nothing. Black must move it or guard it, and that costs a move.

items.prompt: Black to move. Which of these pieces has no legal move at all?

claims.statement: The bishop on f8 has no legal move.
The knight on g8 has one legal move.
The rook on h8 has one legal move.
The knight on b8 has two legal moves.

hints: A piece with no move is blocked by its own pawns or pieces.
Look at the squares next to each piece.
The bishop on f8: e7 and g7 are both occupied by black pawns.
items.explain: The bishop on f8 can only move along diagonals, and both are blocked by its own pawns on e7 and g7. The knight on g8 can go to f6, the rook on h8 to h7, and the knight on b8 to a6 or d7. Black's kingside development is slow; that is part of what White pays the knight for.

items.prompt: Black to move, a knight up (this is the tenth move of the real game). One natural developing move runs into a tactic. Find a queen move the engine prefers at depth 16.

claims.statement: 10...Qc8, 10...Qc7 and 10...Qb6 are all within 70 cp of the engine's top move (depth 16).
10...Nbd7 is at least 150 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).
After 10...Nbd7 11.Nxf7 Kxf7 12.Qf5+ two white pieces, the queen and the bishop on c4, attack the pawn on e6.

hints: Look at the bishop on f7: the knight on e5 attacks it and only the king guards it.
The natural knight move runs into Nxf7 Kxf7 Qf5+, which attacks the pawn on e6 twice. A queen move first avoids that.
The queen steps to c8, c7 or b6.
items.explain: Developing the b8 knight to d7 lets the white knight take on f7. The king must recapture, and the white queen then jumps to f5 with check, attacking e6 with the queen and the bishop. [I] After Bxe6 the knight on d7 is hit as well. A queen move first avoids that: Qc8 adds a guard to e6, and Qc7 and Qb6 keep the knight at home. Engine, depth 16: the three queen moves are close at the top; the knight development is nearly two pawns worse.

feedback_by_move.b8d7: The knight blocks the queen and the next board shows the capture on f7 that wins material.

items.prompt: White to move. Black's last move developed a knight and left something loose. What do you play?

claims.statement: The capture on f7 is the engine's top move (depth 16).
11.f4 is at least 250 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).
11.Qe2 is at least 400 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).
One white piece, the knight on e5, attacks the bishop on f7.
Only one black piece, the king, defends the bishop on f7.
After Nxf7 Kxf7 Qf5+ the queen and the bishop on c4 attack the pawn on e6.

hints: Look at the bishop on f7 and who guards it.
Count the attackers and defenders of the bishop on f7: the knight attacks it and only the king defends it.
The knight takes on f7.
items.explain: The bishop on f7 is attacked by the knight on e5 and defended only by the king; the queen on d8 never guarded f7, because its own pawn on e6 blocks the diagonal. The knight takes, the king must recapture, and then Qf5+ attacks the pawn on e6 with the queen and the bishop on c4. Engine, depth 16: the capture is the clear first choice, and quiet moves such as f4 or Qe2 throw the advantage away.

feedback_by_move.f2f4: A natural-looking move, but it ignores the loose bishop and Black untangles with ...Qc8.
feedback_by_move.d3e2: The queen leaves the diagonal and Black takes the knight on e5.

items.prompt: White to move. Two pieces can take the pawn on e6 with check. The game continued with the queen. Which capture does the engine prefer (depth 16)?

claims.statement: Taking with the bishop on e6, with check, is the engine's top move (depth 16).
Taking with the queen on e6 is at least 150 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: Both captures give check, so look at what each leaves behind.
After the queen captures, the bishop on c4 and the pawn on d4 become targets.
The bishop takes on e6.
items.explain: Both captures win the pawn with check and drive the king to e8. If the queen takes, Black's queen on b6 attacks the pawn on d4 and the bishop on c4 loses its guard, which is how the game went. If the bishop takes, the queen stays on f5 and the bishop keeps its pawn, and White can castle with threats. Engine, depth 16: the bishop capture is the first choice.

feedback_by_move.f5e6: White played this in the game and still won, but the engine shows Black getting counterplay with ...Ke8 and ...Qxd4.

items.prompt: White to move, a knight down. Which move is within 40 centipawns of the engine's top move at depth 16? Two moves qualify; either is accepted.

claims.statement: 8.Ne5 and 8.Bd3 are both within 40 cp of the engine's top move (depth 16).
8.Bc4 is at least 20 cp worse than the best move (depth 16).

hints: White needs to keep making threats and develop at the same time.
One move attacks the loose bishop; another develops and prepares to castle with tempo against the bishop on g6.
The knight goes to e5, or the bishop to d3.
items.explain: The knight on e5 attacks the loose bishop on g6, and the bishop on d3 faces the same bishop along the diagonal and develops. A quiet move such as h3 gives Black time to untangle, and the bishop to c4 allows ...Bf5 with no problem. Engine, depth 16: the knight and bishop moves are about level at the top; the others lose a fifth of a pawn or more.

feedback_by_move.h2h3: A waiting move. Black plays ...Nd7 and ...Qa5+ and the extra knight starts to count.
feedback_by_move.f1c4: The bishop aims at e6, but it threatens nothing at once and is a little worse than the leaders; Black simply develops.
